677.t: Earlier recordings with the Quality Serenaders and Armstrong
677.s: His first recordings were for Victor with Paul Howard's band, then Mosby and Armstrong in Los Angeles in 1930.
677.q: Oh, the first time I ever recorded was in California, on Victor, with the Quality Seranaders, Paul Howard's Quality Seranaders. And then I recorded some with the other fellow, Mosby's. And then we recorded on our own name, Quality Seranaders. Paul -- I mean Lawrence, Charlie Lawrence was the…

677.t: First recordings with the Quality Serenaders
677.s: His first records were for Victor in 1929 with the Quality Serenaders, including Charlie's Idea by Charlie Lawrence.
677.q: Well, the first recordings I would say were around '29 because Louis didn't come here until '30. And it was around '29 and we were -- I was in this band called Quality Serenaders. And we had a contract with Victor. We made about -- what was it -- six, or eight, or ten records

677.t: First Ellington recording, The Sheik of Araby
677.s: His first Ellington session in New York was The Sheik of Araby, with Hodges also soloing, dated May 16, 1932 by the discography.
677.q: The first record I made was "The Sheik," in New York. What -- I'm trying to think of the director's name, the engineer's name. He later became very famous out here in the movies.

677.t: More Armstrong sides, and the gap before Ellington's first record
677.s: He confirms If I Could Be with You belonged to the Armstrong sessions, then recalls weeks of theaters and dances before The Sheik was recorded the week after Easter 1932.
677.q: Well, let's see. In those days we were playing these theaters week after week all the time. It was theaters one after another, and in between would be these

34.t: First recording, Chicago 1925, with Richard M. Jones
34.s: His first date was a 1925 pickup session for OKeh led by pianist Richard M. Jones, with Preston Jackson, Omer Simeon and Jabbo Smith; he cannot recall titles.
34.q: I don't know, but a bunch of musicians that come hired us on an OK record. This guy's name was Richard. Richard Jones. Richard Jones.

34.t: Recording with Joe Liggins and the band personnel
34.s: He made all of Liggins's records and lists the six men who played on them.
34.q: Oh, I made all the records with him.

34.t: Records with Leon Rene in Los Angeles
34.s: He recorded in the early 1930s with Leon Rene's small band, naming sidemen, and says most of his work was in big bands before Liggins.
34.q: i don't forget but i know i made that one with richard jones and uh we made like we made quite a few records out here some with uh leon renee here in los angeles yeah but we had quite a few musicians out here from new orleans you know yeah

279.s: Hug describes the personnel, tunes and difficult conditions of the Roosevelt Hotel session.
279.q: No, my first records were with Shawkey Banana in 1936 when Shawkey Banana came with them. And we were playing together then. Where is the Shawpery? The Shawpery is now called Maison's Beach House out on Ponchacrine Boulevard. Were the records made in New Orleans? Oh, yes. I made the records with…

279.s: Hug lists the band that made the records with Sharkey and why a different band was used.
279.ch: Dance halls and clubs of the 1930s
279.q: Yeah, that was in 36, I believe. Yeah, Sharky was playing. We had Sharky. I think Leo Brookhoven was playing Fitch trumpet. Sharky was playing second trumpet. We had Adrian Gosley playing drums, and Dan McGowan was playing bass.

417.t: Sorting out the discography: first album and joining McDuff in 1963
417.s: Benson corrects discography errors, dates his first Columbia records, and confirms his first album as a leader was The New Boss Guitar and that he joined McDuff in 1963.
417.q: And the wrong time. Our first records with Columbia were made in late ’65 or early ’66 with John Hammond. Those titles you mentioned were on there. It was – Clockwise was one of the songs.

417.t: Mona Lisa on ukulele and the four RCA sides
417.s: He explains the seven-year-old Mona Lisa recording made at a union-run studio, how he uses it in his Nat Cole show, and which titles were cut at the 1954 RCA session.
417.ch: Teen bandleader and the road to McDuff
417.q: Oh yeah, yeah. Somebody recorded – I think it was my manager – or agent, Eugene Landy. I was in his office one day. He had an office, downtown Pittsburgh. He had a couple of artists. He had a – it was another older singer. He sang a lot like – the only person I can compare him to today would be…

576.t: George Russell's tape leads to the Blue Note record
576.s: Russell shops her tape to Blue Note and Mercury; Blue Note signs her, with Quincy Jones's later letter, and she gets guitar, Denzil Best and Steve Swallow.
576.ch: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
576.q: the meantime, that was my very first, you know, professional recording. And then right after that, he paid to have a tape made―George Russell―of me singing songs that, all the songs that are on this Blue Note. That was George. George got that record date. He peddled this around to, to two different…

576.t: George Russell hears her and records her singing You Are My Sunshine
576.s: George Russell hears her at the Page Three, visits her grandmother's Pennsylvania mining club with her, and has her sing You Are My Sunshine on his Outer View record, her first professional recording.
576.ch: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
576.q: Love For Sale. Okay? So then, during the, during the Monday night sessions, we‟d have different piano players and they were all good. So we had this one piano player, Jack Riley, who would play on Monday nights. So his teacher came down to hear him on a Monday night, and the teacher‟s name was…

493.t: Recording at fourteen: Heart of Gold and Pontius Pilate's Decision
493.s: He played a standard on his father's album and, despite doubts about his age, practiced to be on Delfeayo's RCA Novus record. Brown recalls seeing him at Jazz Fest.
493.ch: Return to New Orleans and the early scene
493.q: That album – so now, I’m starting to record. It’s funny, because at the time of the demo, I did some tunes with my father for an album called Heart of Gold. We recorded two songs, one of which got released. I think it was This Can’t Be Love. It was just a standard that I played with him. I think it…

493.t: The week of the Pontius Pilate sessions with Branford
493.s: He describes the January 1992 sessions in New York. Branford was recording a blues record the same week and Jason stayed at his place.
493.ch: Return to New Orleans and the early scene
493.q: Yeah. It was after – when was that? I’m going to – I’m drawing a blank, because I remember it. You know what? It was later that year. I’ll tell a little bit of a story about the Pontius Pilate’s Decision session, because it was January of ’92. It’s a good story in terms of just the week of that…

228.t: His first record, with Charlie Singleton's rhythm-and-blues band
228.s: McLean played baritone on Camel Walkin' for Singleton in New York around 1947-48, before Dig.
228.ch: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
228.q: No, that was another one. That was the first record that I ever made, period. That was a rhythm-and-blues thing with Charlie Singleton’s band. I wasn’t – didn’t play any solos on it. I played baritone on that.

228.s: McLean says New Soil, not Jackie's Bag, was his first Blue Note record.
228.ch: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
228.q: No. The first one was New Soil.

426.t: Recording for Gus Statiras's Progressive label
426.s: He recorded early sessions for the Progressive label in the early 1950s, not knowing how the connection was made.
426.q: Yeah, I wasn’t partied to that, you understand, I wasn’t present as to who said what to whom. As far as I know, I recorded it for Gus Deterris, for a label called…

426.t: Getting the first engineer credit on Tristano's Jazz label single
426.s: Tristano's 'Ju Ju' / 'Pastime' single on his own Jazz label (Jazz 101) credited Rudy, the first engineer credit.
426.q: Yeah that one was called, “Ju Ju”, ’78, single. “Pastime” I think was the name of the other song, and he started his own label called “Jazz.” He put my name as an engineer on the label, and that was first time any engineer gotten credit.

64.t: First recordings with Foots Thomas and his Savoy date
64.s: His first records were with Walter Foots Thomas alongside veterans, then his first date under his own name for Savoy.
64.ch: New York scene and bebop community
64.q: It was my first recording under my name. I had actually recorded with Foots Thomas and some other people on records with them.

64.t: Early records with Foots Thomas and the Slam Stewart Quartet
64.s: He explains his earliest professional records and replacing Errol Garner in Slam Stewart's group, which became a quartet.
64.ch: Sideman years and the European tour
64.q: That was much later. In the records that we were looking through a moment ago, there was something… Walter Foots Thomas… those were the first records that I ever made in a professional sense. Those were the very first records I made and after that point I actually made some recordings… I tried to…

66.t: Her first solo record for Jack Kapp
66.s: She went to Chicago where Kapp recorded her playing what she thought was an audition. 'Night Life' became her first record, for which she was never paid.
66.ch: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
66.q: I went back to Kansas City with the band and then Andy Kirk received a wire for them to come to Chicago. They went without me. They left me in Kansas City and what I did was join them because Jack Capp wouldn't record them without me.

66.t: Recording with Blanche Calloway and the Brunswick date
66.s: She sorts out the order of events: Blanche Calloway's Victor session came first, then the Pearl Theatre, then Brunswick refused to record Kirk unless she was there.
66.ch: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
66.q: I think that's when they had changed it to Blanche Calloway. Victor had recorded her like that also, Blanche Calloway and her band.

388.t: Begin the Beguine session and the Lincoln Hotel sensation
388.s: The Spring 1938 sessions produce 'Begin the Beguine', 'Back Bay Shuffle' and 'Indian Love Call'; the hit saves the band, which reopens the Lincoln Hotel and films a short.
388.q: And we left town, he was thinking of dissolving the band, but he had a commitment in a hotel in St. Louis and he couldn't take Billie Holiday down there,

388.t: Joe Turner's 'The Boss of the Blues' session with Kansas City veterans
388.s: Called to a Carnegie Hall rehearsal-room date, Leeman finds Joe Turner, Pete Johnson, Pete Brown, Lawrence Brown and Freddie Green, the only white player, in a record later ranked among the best.
388.q: I've got to get to one of the most exciting record dates, and a definite high point in my career. I was called by -- I don't remember whom, to do a record date while I was on the Hit Parade, and I had a record in front of me, and if you wait until I research, I'll give you the year.

428.t: First record date with Red Allen at the Ritz Brothers songs
428.s: Hall recalls his first legal record date and its personnel.
428.q: Yeah, and Red Allen -- let's see. Red had -- he was in Lou Russell's band. That's what it was -- at the Savoy Ballroom -- when I made my first legal record date with Red Allen and we did -- I think it was on Vocalian -- the Ritz Brothers, songs of their show, 'He Ain't Got Rhythm' and things like…

428.t: Recording with Louis Jordan's Tympany Five for Decca
428.s: Hall became Decca's house bass player after Jordan's first dates and recalls tunes and Jordan's earlier career.
428.ch: The craft of the ad lib player
428.q: Well, then that becomes an ego thing. I remember working the first dates bass with Louis Jordan's band. The original Timpany Five, He didn't have a bass player on (inaudible) just for records, and I was chosen for Decca. And the engineers at Decca said I had the most perfect beat of all the rest of…

77.t: Running Wild, Cecil Mack and an early record with a choir
77.s: She remembers Running Wild and recalls making one of the first records with a choir behind singer Elkins, probably for Black Swan.
77.ch: New Orleans musicians, recordings and radio
77.q: Uh-huh, well, Running -- yes, I remember Running Wild well. Let me see. Cecil Mack, you know, collaborated with Eubie Blake in writing a lot of his music, because he wrote -- oh, I remember the first record that was made with a choir. I made it with a fellow named Elkins, and he had a big choir…

77.t: Lovie at the Monogram Theater; where Hunter recorded
77.s: Lovie played piano at the packed Monogram vaudeville house; Hunter's Paramount sessions were mostly in New York, with a couple with Lovie in Chicago in 1923, including her own "Experience Blues".
77.ch: Records, Lovie Austin and a first marriage
77.q: Yeah, very small but packed to capacity at all times, and they did nine and ten shows, and each house was packed. Now, she would -- this -- had this little funny upright piano sitting down, and she'd look up at the people. That's the way she'd do when she would -- it was a vaudeville -- little…

172.t: The first Tuxedo Band records and who played
172.s: Tunes recorded (Careless Love, Black Rag, Original Tuxedo Rag, Hoey Nelly), personnel, and the drummer Chinee's slide whistle.
172.q: Manuel Minetti, piano. William Ridgely, Celestine. Johnny Sincer. Tom Benton. Chani on drum. Samuel Memorero on bass violin. John Marrero, guitar.

920.t: Katherine Dunham engagement and the Commodore session
920.s: Edwards's work with Katherine Dunham with Hackett, then how the Commodore date was run, with Davison and Kaminsky.
920.q: yes yes that was a excellent engagement played around and I played in the pit played on stage that's where I might I run into these uh uh various musicians around the country you could just tell

241.t: First recording session with Bill Russell
241.s: He recalls his first record for Bill Russell, financed by Alden and David, and the substitute trombonist after Robert Thomas could not come.
241.q: You know, people asked me for, a girl like me, they said, you wasn't nice when you first made the regards. I said, no I wasn't. What was you gonna be nice for? First of all, you see, I said, just run into it, they don't know, don't worry about it, you know what I mean? You know, annoying, being…

689.t: Jelly Roll Martin and the London Blues recording with Buster Bailey and Zutty Robinson
689.s: Dominique recorded London Blues and Sunday Sweetheart with Jelly Roll Martin, Buster Bailey, a nervous Zoo Robinson and others.
689.q: Sunday Sweetheart. That's the time Buster Bailey, Zoo Robinson. We had Johnny Sincere guitar. Who was playing bass? I think Bill Johnson was playing bass. I'm not mistaken. The Jellarole Martin.

82.t: First Memphis Five date, Paramount, and the California Ramblers
82.s: He made the Memphis Five's first date for Paramount, auditioned the California Ramblers there, and recorded them under about twenty pseudonyms. He mentions his diaries and the Harlem Nest club's influence.
82.q: No, I think I made their first date for them, and we then freelanced around. I think that the first date was for the Paramount Records, which was an independent company at the time.

1030.t: First records with Brownlee in New Orleans
1030.s: Sharkey recalls his first record date and working with Brownlee, the only band he did not lead; Brownlee as salesman and pianist.
1030.ch: Early New Orleans bands and records
1030.q: An okay record made. Yeah, it was on Barone Street in Greenwalls. Had you been working with Brownlee for a while, or? Yes, Brownlee was the only band that I wasn't the leader of. After that, I started off as a leader, and then I went to work with Brownlee for a while, and then I organized my band…

761.t: First record with Celestin and the band personnel
761.s: He made 'My Josephine' with Celestin and lists the large band, singers and trombonists.
761.q: No. I made a few homemade records like my brother Boy now. But the first record I really made that worked while I was one with Celestan. I made the Josephine with Celestan. He made two Josephines. I think I made one and Jeanette made one. First of Sam and Ryan.

38.t: Recording for Mayo Williams of Decca
38.s: Levy made records for Mayo Williams on tenor guitar and was ashamed of the tunes chosen.
38.q: I made, yes, I hate to tell about it. No, we had, during the time that we had this little string band, I wrote a tune and carried it down to Mayo Williams who was with Decca. And Mayo said, who is that, whipping that guitar? I said, that's me playing guitar. I said, but that's a tenor guitar. I…

653.t: First recordings in 1953 with Champion Jack Dupree and Christine Kittrell
653.s: His first recording was in 1953 for King with Champion Jack Dupree, and the same year he played bass on a Nashville date.
653.ch: On the road and into brass bands
653.q: Yeah. You know, he did it there. But we didn't record that with him. We recorded the answer to King... ...to Song된 stuff. ...Stług된 stuff... Stług된 stuff... Stług

152.t: First recordings with Bartholomew, Smiley Lewis and Fats Domino
152.s: He recalls his first recordings, a split Fats Domino session with Jewel King where he played the solo, and learning the disc-recording process.
152.ch: Dave Bartholomew band and early recording
152.q: Well, I think that might have been after we had done some things with Smiley Lewis. Maybe I'm wrong. I don't know. But that first recording with Fats Domino was a split session. Fats Domino had a split session with a lady by the name of Jill King. Mm-hmm. She had the hit record called Three Times…

23.t: First recording sessions: the Andrews Sisters booth and the Dan Burley date
23.s: Rose describes helping in the booth at an Andrews Sisters session where he met Bobby Hackett, and his first own session, Dan Burley's Chicken Shack Shuffle.
23.q: Well, my first recording session that I worked on in any capacity at all, uh, which is strange, was, uh, uh, on a recording of the Andrew Sisters by Mir Bistachain, which, uh, uh, the first session that I made under my own aegis, as it were, was a record of Dan Burley called Chicken Shack Shuffled,…

675.t: His first record and early recording opportunities
675.s: Braud says his first records were Bremen Hand Breakdown and Black and Tan Fantasy, and that Mamie Smith was first to record.
675.q: None of those guys. No, none of those guys wasn't recording. We didn't have the opportunity to record. We had the right material, but... We just didn't have the opportunity to record at that time.

866.t: Making his first record with Punch Miller
866.s: Angrum recalls recording for the first time two days earlier at Royal and Ursulines with Punch Miller, and how nervous he was.
866.q: Yeah. Two days ago. You played with the Sheik? Punch Miller. Punch Miller. Yeah. How did you like that section? I liked that section very well. It was a good section. You didn't get nervous? Well, I was nervous on the first. When I was starting off, I wasn't nervous. I was real nervous. I was…

49.t: First recording with Johnny Hyman and the Red Nichols style
49.s: His first record was with Johnny Hyman, with named players, patterned on Red Nichols's 'futuristic' music.
49.ch: Mellophone, Brunswick records and the West End Roof
49.q: I don't know. I don't know. Maybe some of the ones that we made up at WSMB. But this was for Victor. Yeah. Uh, Alligator Crawl. And that band was Dias, Horace Dias on piano. Nappy LeMond on the guitar. Elroy Mays on clarinet. Charlie Hartman on trombone. Johnny and myself. And, and, and, huh? A…

287.t: First Chicago recordings and the band with Bobby Jones
287.s: His first engagements were record dates with the Dodds brothers and Frank Melrose, then he formed an eight-piece band with Bobby Jones. He later made a Paramount session with accordion and Joe Wiggins.
287.ch: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
287.q: Yeah. Well, that's hard to tell, my first engagement, because I had to make myself known. I wasn't known at all in Chicago. I see. See, so I say my first engagement were recording with Baby Dots and Johnny Dots and Frank Melrose, piano player.

924.s: Jones recalls McDonald's New York dates, his years on the road with a flower company, and the band's fame, but is unsure about their recordings.
924.q: Yeah, he'd been to New York, played the Hippodrome Theater, several games in New York for Charles Dillian Yes, I remember that name.

633.t: First recording with a brass band
633.s: His only recording was with a brass band, apparently with George Lewis, made with little rehearsal.
633.q: They didn't have much of a bass on them. The fellas just jumped up and made them records, you know? They didn't practice. The bass player, he didn't have no amateur. They had no bamboo

642.t: Recalling the 1936 hotel meeting and Guesnon's first record
642.s: Guesnon recalls 1936 when he made his first record, 'Goodbye, Good Luck to You'; Montgomery says he had urged him, and Guesnon admits he feared recording.
642.q: Yeah, goodbye, good luck to you was a good number, I'd been trying to get you to make it all the time, but you scared, you know, you'd shy or something, I don't know...

820.t: A scratch recording session with Von Gammon on drums
820.s: Frank describes a no-name, no-pay jam recording with Perranti, Charlie Hartman and Von Gammon, playing bass.
820.q: It was a piano player that used to work more or less by himself down back in those days. Could have been Joe Wolf.

289.t: Nashville audition and first recording of Slim
289.s: A Nashville club owner heard the band in Monroe and brought it up; they won a four-week contract and Slim recorded his first song, Feeling Sad, for a small label.
289.q: So we did, we went on to that term. And the night we got there, Diana Watson and Illinois Jackie was playing. You can remember them, they were playing together. So after they went off, the show went off, and we came on, I don't know, people just went, they went wild and see that guy, that little…

127.t: His first record and Henry Brown
127.s: The first record 'Black but Sweet' with the Macs, made in New Orleans; talk of pianist Henry Brown.
127.q: I forgot where that was, but I don't believe it was on Cornell Street. I believe it was on either Barone or Carnell Street, something like that. It probably was Barone. Hmm? Probably was Barone, because I think Manuel Moneta made some records at the same time.

951.t: Hammer ring track and Oster's first recording visit
951.s: They play the hammer ring song, whose lead singer is on the record cover, and recall it as the first song sung when the professor first came.
951.q: 59. Correction is 59. Yeah. Correction is 59. I got transferred here. Okay. Let's take a listen to this third band here. That's your hammer ring. He's going to be on here if you can put it on there. Right there. Big wide one there. Oh, that's it. I'll get it. Yeah, there it is. Right there.

831.t: First recording sessions: Brunis, Shockey, Almerico
831.s: His first recording was with Abby Brunis; later he recorded with Shockey and Almerico.
831.q: Yeah, after I left Bruner. Uh huh. Yeah, I made some records with Shockey. I think I made some with Shockey. I made some with Al Marika. That's about all. Remember any of the tunes you made with Shockey? Huh? Remember any tunes you made with Shockey? No, I don't remember any of them.

15.t: W.C. Handy takes a Chicago-augmented band to New York for Columbia
15.s: Handy brought a band including Howard and violinist Willie Tyler to New York to make 33 sides for Columbia.
15.q: Uh-huh. Very fine violinist. Myself, I was about five or six of us put in a band. Went to New York, made 33 sides for the Columbia people.

128.t: Sam Morgan band's 1924 record and its personnel
128.s: Robinson recalls the band's single recording session in 1924, who was in the band, and the tunes, including a hymn.
128.q: With Sam's band or...? Yeah, with Sam's band. Me making them records in... ...2024. 1924, huh? 1924. That's where I could... ...where I could get to. 24. 24.

140.t: Grimes's first recordings and early start
140.s: Rowe asks about Grimes's first dates around 1957 with Shafi Hadi (Curtis Porter), Adams and Kelly; Ali notes Grimes started early.
140.q: See ‘cause Henry was a little more advanced than I was. Henry started playing with the big timers before I even thought about leaving out of Philadelphia. He did it really fast. Man this cat was, he was something else.

495.t: First record and the number of sessions he played
495.s: His most important first record was with Mike Moore; a website listed five hundred to a thousand records he played on.
495.q: And it had my name and all the records I’d been on. And it was like, it must have been five hundred to a thousand.

206.t: Dick Hyman and the first recording under his own name
206.s: Hyman brought him to an Esoteric date and became his key to New York work.
206.q: Dick Hyman and I became friends and he — well that’s how I did my very first recording under my own name. He took me on a date to play behind a singer. I don’t even think I had anything written down. He said well just play it, and then play a solo for eight bars here or something. That was Esoteric…

420.t: First record date for Chiaroscuro with Bob Wilber
420.s: Wilber heard them at Condon's and organised the first record with the Hamilton quartet; Flanigan criticises its direct-pickup sound.
420.q: That was something that Bob Wilber instigated for the Chiaroscuro label. He heard us play at Eddie Condon’s and he was blown away that all these young guys — we were all under 25 then I guess — were playing this style music, so he got a date and he put — the original quartet, which was without…

497.t: First recordings: Japanese date, India Navigation and Contemporary
497.s: He recorded three albums within months, in Chicago for a Japanese label, for India Navigation, and for Contemporary with Elvin Jones.
497.q: That’s kind of interesting. I kind of recorded three albums almost simultaneously. It was a little unusual. The ACAM, which is the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians, had garnered some attention from the Japanese in Chicago, and there were some Japanese record companies that were…

466.t: First New York record date with Mat Matthews
466.s: His first date, produced by accordionist Mat Matthews with studio stars; he read every written-out triplet of 'Prisoner of Love' and the band laughed.
466.ch: New York studio and sideman work
466.q: Because I remember who the band was. It was astonishing. It was — the drummer was Osie Johnson and the bass player was Wendell Marshall. I played piano. A guy by the name of Everett Barksdale played guitar. Clark Terry. Big Nick Nicholas was the tenor player, Jerome Richardson, and somebody else.…

324.t: Allen Eager record date, Teddy Reig and Duke Jordan's Jordu
324.s: At his first big record date Gibbs did not know the Jordu release changes, Duke Jordan wouldn't help, and Teddy Reig stormed into the booth.
324.q: Yeah. [inaudible] I think it was my first big record date with Allen Eager. Allen Eager — you know who Teddy “Fats” Reig was? Teddy Reig was the first guy to ever record Bird and Diz, for Savoy Records. He ran that company. And Teddy weighed about 400 pounds. And Allen Eager was the hot white tenor…

670.t: First record date with Leonard Feather
670.s: She recalls the Black and White session with Feather on piano, Georgie Auld, Barney Bigard and a drummer, and later labels.
670.q: Yeah, the pianist didn’t show up so Leonard Feather had to play piano. And it was Georgie Auld on tenor, and it was, the bassist was, his son is named Pickles, I can’t think of his name right now. But it was all top notch musicians, and Georgie Auld on tenor and clarinet was —

336.t: First recording with Milt Hinton and Carmen Cavallaro
336.s: His first record, aged 18 in 1961, for Decca with Cavallaro, guided by Milt Hinton; Rowe takes his birth date.
336.q: Yeah. I was with Carmen Cavallaro for a year, at 18, and hanging on by the skin of my teeth you know. Because it was demanding. It wasn’t a real jazz gig but it was like he carried a quartet. I mean piano, bass, drums and guitar. He carried three other musicians beside himself. And he had a show…

159.t: Not liking his own records; first album Junior with Ray Brown
159.s: Self-criticism, and his first Verve album as leader with Ray Brown and Lex Humphries.
159.q: With myself? I could be. That’s what everybody says. But I don’t know why I’m like that. I listen to my records like in the studio and I may listen to like the rough draft of it,

554.t: First records: Undercurrent Blues and Sam Most Plus Two
554.s: His first 45 with Dick Hyman, and the 1954 session with Bellson and Percy Heath that Mingus issued on Debut.
554.q: That’s the one I’m talking about, yeah. Here and there I meet somebody that says “you know I have a copy of that ‘Undercurrent Blues.’” But I don’t know where my copy is.

351.t: First record date with Kai Winding, Shelly Manne and Allen Eager
351.s: His first professional date, arranged by Teddy Reig, was tense because of Allen Eager and ran overnight.
351.q: Savoy Records, Guild Records, whatever. And he called me and my first record date was, are you ready for this? My first record date, Kay [sic] Winding, or Kai as he was known later, Shelly Manne, Ed Safranski, and Allen, boy, I just drew a blank.

162.t: First record date with Red Norvo and Mildred Bailey
162.s: After the union transfer wait, George Wettling brought him to a Norvo session where he soloed on two tunes; he lost his copies.
162.q: Well let’s see. I went into New York so I transferred in so you had to — when you transferred in, I’ll make this real short — you’re not allowed to work a steady job for the first three months. Otherwise everybody’d come to New York you know what I mean? But they made it difficult. After three…

1004.t: Her album Born to Be Blue and its rediscovery
1004.s: Through Joe Reisman at Roulette she recorded her first album at 23, later rediscovered by an engineer and reissued on CD.
1004.q: But the best thing that happened on something that wasn’t one of those, I was at Dick Charles’ studio. And he called me up and said, “I think there’s an elderly man who’s written a lot of music for the Kraft Music Hall themes and stuff, Vladimir Solinsky. And

353.t: First recording, Bird Calls for United Artists
353.s: Sitting in with Art Blakey led Alan Douglas to record her, and Leonard Feather's idea produced Bird Calls with Leroy Vinnegar and Russ Freeman.
353.q: My first opportunity to record was in 1962 I believe. Leonard Feather came to hear me play one time. He was very impressed with my playing. And then Art Blakey, my former husband, Richie Goldberg, was a drummer, and he knew all the musicians from back east, and when he came out here, we married out…

450.t: First record: Moody's 'Le Vent Vert' in Paris
450.s: Her first record was a wordless 78 written by James Moody, made in Paris.
450.q: When I went to Paris. I was living in Paris and Moody, James Moody, had written a tune with no words, which was kind of prophetic in a way, because I’ve sung many songs without words, and it was called “Le Vent Vert” and that was the very first time I ever made a record.

548.s: He paid about $5,000 for an all-original modern album with Brecker, McNealy, Goldsby and Washington.
548.q: To an extent, although I think the more adventuresome stuff that I’ve done has not been recorded. Some of it I’m starting to. Again, to back up, it’s 1985 when I was working with Benny Goodman and almost all my work was in that swing-Dixieland kind of stuff. I financed my own first record, just…

164.t: Dorsey, Kenton and the Shearing style at Discovery Records
164.s: Clarifying his dates with Dorsey, he explains playing block chords learned from sax voicings, which got him Discovery Records work.
164.q: No I never worked with Louie’s big band. I never worked with him there. Dorsey I was with in ’47 and ’48, and then ’49 I came out and starred for a year with the rest of the Kenton guys. They couldn’t get into the studios either for the first year or so. I mean I came in with a reputation as being…

489.t: Recording Walk Tall with Bennie Maupin and Harvey Mason
489.s: Walk Tall was his first record; Keepnews told him to get who he wanted and he chose Bennie Maupin and Harvey Mason. He discusses the solo-with-drums passage.
489.q: Uh huh. Yeah. Well that was how I wanted it. That was pretty much it. And you know to this day I mean I enjoy that kind of playing, you know where I’m just soloing with one other person you know. And I still love to do that.

361.t: First recordings with Terry Gibbs and Herb Ellis
361.s: His first album was with Terry Gibbs, the second with Herb Ellis.
361.q: Oh, the first one I recorded with was Terry Gibbs. And in a lifetime of playing you do a lot of recordings, it’s all part of the business you know. And I remember the first one as well as I remember yesterday. I may have forgotten a whole bunch of them, which I have, but you don’t forget the first…

671.t: First recordings during the record strike
671.s: His first records were with Eckstine during the Petrillo recording strike.
671.q: Well I don’t know. We walked up many, many flights of steps to the studio. Petrillo had everybody closed up back in those days.

1049.t: Getting signed as the first GRP artist
1049.s: Through a demo session with Noel Pointer, Larry Rosen heard him and Dave Grusin called to offer a record.
1049.q: Well I went to school with Noel Pointer and he had called me up and said he was doing a demo session, but he couldn’t pay me. So he said you can bring down a tune, and we’ll record it and you can keep the demo. I said all right, fine. So I brought down a tune called “Rain Storm.” And after I…

611.t: First recordings and the Charlie Johnson's Paradise Ten session
611.s: His first record was made in Philadelphia for a pioneer like Perry Bradford; the Victor session with Charlie Johnson's Paradise Ten used his arrangements, including his own Harlem Drag.
611.q: No, I made my first recording in Philadelphia way before that. But I, myself have never heard it. I made it for a guy named Perry, Perry Bradford I think or something like that. I can’t, I forget his name a little bit. He was a kind of pioneer in recording in those days. He recorded the famous…

448.t: The Wildcats and recording for Commodore
448.s: He formed The Wildcats with Fife, Wellstood and Traeger, won over Milt Gabler at Jimmy Ryan's and recorded four sides.
448.q: Yeah. I was playing with these older fellas and then I gradually found out about other musicians around the county. Eddie Fife was in Larchmont and up in Greenwich Connecticut there was a piano player, Dick Wellstood, and the bass player, Charlie Traeger. And out of this group we gradually had jam…

85.t: First recordings with Charlie Johnson in 1928
85.s: Berger reminds him of his first documented recordings, two arrangements among four tunes.
85.q: You Ain’t the One. I don’t remember that.

223.t: First recording date with Ike Carpenter
223.s: Discussion of his first documented session, the clarinet squeak on Dancers in Love and the a&r man's remark.
223.q: Part of it is. Dancers in Love, which is the Duke [Ellington]. He had a lot of Duke‟s voicings down. He knew a lot of the repertoire. So I guess he wrote that chart. It had a clarinet part which – I‟ve never been a great clarinet player. Every time we would play that chart, I would squeak on the…

703.t: First recordings and the hunt for the funky pianist
703.s: Brown reads his early discography while Bobby and Rosemary try to remember the pianist on This is the Blues.
703.q: No, real big. Short, heavy. He had Ron Jefferson and Leroy Vinnegar.

368.t: First recordings and Dorsey calling him away from Barnet
368.s: He made no solos with Barnet; his first real solo recording was Opus One with Dorsey, who called him in 1943.
368.q: Yeah, yeah. I think it was Charlie Barnet. Yeah, I think it was Barnet’s band that he called.

558.t: First US recording with Machito and Mario Bauza
558.s: Playing the Tanga theme on the La Conga radio broadcast led Machito's orchestra to invite him to record El Rey del Mambo in 1946.
558.q: Well, the musical director of Machito's orchestra was his brother in law, Mario Bauza, who was married to Machito’s sister, the singer Graciela. So then the recording was made possible because just when I was working at the Cabaret La Conga with the dancing couple I mentioned before, Carmen and…

105.t: His first recording and never being nervous
105.s: Asked about his first record, with Slim Gaillard, Hamilton says he never gets nervous because playing is simply what he does.
105.q: I’ve never been nervous. I’ve never been nervous when I’ve got to play. That’s what I do. Ain’t nothing to get nervous about, you know.

515.t: First recordings: Montego Joe, Mongo and Tones For Joan's Bones
515.s: Panken and Corea sort out which recording was his first.
515.q: That’s what I’m told. Either that, or the Mongo Santamaria that I did, called Go, Mongo.

369.t: Her first recording session for Victor/Bluebird with Mayo Williams
369.s: She cut Piano Boogie and Everyday Blues; the sessions took two or three takes, and she recalls the Baldwin baby grand and her preference for a nine-foot Steinway.
369.q: They wanted me to record on Decca. I recorded a lot of things for Decca but they never released them.

107.t: Recording opportunities and the Two Franks
107.s: Joe Newman got him on Jazz Studio One, Benny Powell became an ally, and No Count Basie and the Two Franks records followed.
107.ch: Joining Basie and life on the road
107.q: Frank Wess came a few weeks before I joined. At the time I joined I didn’t know how long he’d been there, but I know it couldn’t have been too long, because Paul Quinichette had been in that chair before

491.t: First recordings: Bullmoose Jackson and Golson's first date as leader
491.s: He recorded I'll Be Home for Christmas with Bullmoose Jackson and Dameron, then led his first date for Contemporary in Los Angeles and was paid $500.
491.ch: Reflections, marriage and early road bands
491.q: Yes. He was recording for the King label, out of Cincinnati. What had been happening – when Bullmoose would record, they would use studio musicians. They wanted to be sure they got exactly what they wanted to get, that would sell. But we were of the mind, if we are the band that’s playing with him…

328.t: The family band's King Records session
328.s: Brower reads the 1953 session details; Hampton recalls two sides, the 78 release and the personnel.
328.ch: Carnegie Hall, bebop and the big bands
328.q: No, I never recorded with Eddie. I would like to have. I know that Eddie was recording with King Records at one time, and we recorded with the family band on King, but we only recorded two sides, because we weren’t really – we didn’t have something that was really valuable enough for them.

135.t: Early records: Paris with McGhee, Dizzy's DG label and Kenny Burrell's first date
135.s: Heath looks back on his first recordings after a year and a half of playing, including Paris sessions, Bud Powell, and Dizzy's date with Joe Carroll.
135.q: Right, and I made an album with him and Kenny, and we tried to make an album with Bud Powell, who was over there by that time. And Norman Granz said, “Aww you’ll never heard this!” ‘cause Bud would skip places and it was [a] really mumbo­ jumbo record. So those are my early, recorded experiences,…

111.t: First recording with Thad Jones and Billy Mitchell
111.s: He describes recording for David Usher's label in a noisy second-floor studio, uneasy with microphones, and the uncertain date.
111.q: I don’t think so. You know maybe it was. I don’t know whether that’s correct. You know the Bluebird is still there! I could call ‘em up and ask them to look it up in the book! (Laughs)

372.t: The January 1949 session under Lennie's name
372.s: They go through the tunes recorded, with Shelly Manne, and Konitz's recollection of the date.
372.ch: The Tristano group and leaving for Kenton
372.q: “Progression”. I think . . . that was based on another one. I think that was based on “Lullaby”, no not “Lullaby”. [sings melody]

460.t: First recording: Tom McIntosh's Great Day with James Moody
460.s: Laws recalls his first session, Moody's Great Day arranged by Tom McIntosh, where flute was written as colour on top of the trumpets. He met McIntosh at a religious meeting.
460.ch: Mongo Santamaria and early recording sessions
460.q: Yeah, okay. My first recording session was with – Tom McIntosh invited me to play on that recording session. Esmond Edwards was the producer on that date. Mac just told me, not too long ago, a conversation he had with Moody about that recording session. He said, “Hubert, I was talking to Moody.” He…

226.t: Bass on Erroll Garner's first record and carrying the bass up 40 flights
226.s: Levy played Garner's first record for Savoy during an elevator strike and demanded extra pay to carry his bass up.
226.q: That’s right. That was his first recording as a leader and his first recording on a record label, which was Savoy. That was the first thing he’d ever recorded. He did – I understand he did

555.s: She recalls Dexter Gordon, her school friend, coaxing her to play without music on his record, her first recording.
555.q: He and I were in school together. He was a bad, bad tenor player, all the time. He was breaking this record. I said, “I’m not – no, no.” He said, “Come on.”

705.s: He explains the Egyptian term 'the first time' and the trio session with Alex Blake and Neil Clarke.
705.q: The recording was…I had my regular guys: Alex Blake and Neil Clark. “Zep Tepi” is an ancient Egyptian word, it means “the first time”. It’s when the creator decided to give us music, because it was a time when there was just silence, there was nothing. Then the whole process of creation took place.…

506.t: His first album as a leader, Where?
506.s: Carter names the personnel on his first record, then jokes about not having read his own biography.
506.q: Called Where? with Eric Dolphy, Mal Waldron, Charlie Persip, and George Duvivier. Nice record.

553.t: First recording date for Savoy in 1955
553.s: His first recording as leader, made on off nights at Hackensack with Wilbur Harden and others.
553.ch: Flute, world instruments and first recordings
553.q: Uh it was Ernie Farrell on bass, Hugh Lawson–piano. Will Austin–bass, Louis Hayes–drums. Um...it was uh Wilbur Harden...

80.t: Fats Waller hears him at Small's and sends for him
80.s: Fats saw him in the club; drummer Arnold Bolling and Bud Scripp woke him at home to ask him to record with Fats at Victor.
80.q: Very fine drummer. He was with -- Arnold played some with everybody. Wait a minute, some of the big bands, a lot of the big bands. Wait a minute. Dog-gone it, I don't know where I am. (Snaps fingers.) Some of the bigger -- Don Redman Bradman. He played with -- what the heck, Arnold played with some…

1.t: Lu's first records: A Tisket, A Tasket at Vocalion
1.s: Lu says Danny was with Cab just over seven years, and she recorded with Cozy Cole and an early Hammond organ at Vocalion.
1.ch: Lu Barker and the Barbarin family
1.q: Not in New York. You know, I sang around here in the bands. But in New York in 1938... I used to sing when Danny would be playing his guitar. So they told him as good as I can sing, why don't you bring me...you know, let them hear me sing. So they brought me down to Vocalion Records.

26.t: Early recordings and recording under different names
26.s: Greer discusses early records including 'Creole Love Call' with Adelaide Hall.
26.ch: Building the band, Ivie Anderson and touring
26.q: Oh, yeah, we recorded -- we recorded, not just under Duke's name. We would cut the band up and record with different people. But I -- and we made so many records, it's hard to recollect now. It's impossible.

87.s: His first recording was with Earl Hines in Chicago around 1933; he hopes Stanley Dance can help with his book.
87.q: I don't know but I got the album home. We did it in Chicago. Yeah, we did. I forgot what label it was but I got the album home.

67.s: His first recording was with Ma Rainey on soprano sax with Wynn's small band; he found her nice and also mentions Lovie Austin.
67.q: I do not remember the tunes. I heard them over in London, John Chilton has that record, I never heard the record, only --

68.t: His first recording date: the 1947 Los Angeles session with Witherspoon
68.s: Tate leads his first date before the recording ban, with C.Q. Price singing blues, Jimmy Witherspoon, and the Supreme label.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: You know, they had a record ban for two years. Oh, and I had C.Q. Price and Emmett Berry, Ted Donnelly, Chico and a very good guitarist by the name of Louis Springer. I didn't find out where he was until -- what's the boy that

409.t: First record session, as Jabbo Smith's replacement
409.s: He was told to stand in on the James P. Johnson record for the missing Jabbo Smith, and was introduced to the studio as Jabbo.
409.q: Yeah. They came by and said, 'Now, listen, Cootie, now you've got to take Jabbo's place, because we can't find him.' Me and Jabbo was two good buddies. And then, 'You are Jabbo. When you get down to the recording studio, we're going to call you Jabbo.'

166.t: Joining Erroll Garner and the first Ralph Bass records
166.s: He joined Garner in New York after the late 1948 Los Angeles sessions sold to Savoy.
166.ch: Erroll Garner, the 1952 arrest and Florida
166.q: They weren't on a label. See, Ralph Bass just give us a record date and he took the masters and sold them to Savoy.

380.t: Andre Previn's first record date at Radio Recorders
380.s: He says he and Irving Ashby backed the 17-year-old Previn in 1946 and recalls engineer Val Valentin and a Goodman session in the same studio.
380.q: No, I don't see it listed here at all. I saw something listed that they didn't know who the bass and drums were, but it was Irving Ashby and me...

381.t: First recording with Roy Eldridge: Muskrat Ramble and High Society
381.s: Learning to read music, and his first recording, on Vocalion, with Don Redman arrangements.
381.ch: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
381.q: Yeah, well they used to play checkers between sets, and so Roy would make me go in the room next door, and get the music book, and learn how to read music -- because also, you know, we had arrangements that were written by some great arrangers back in those days, like Don Redman -- you know, like…

382.t: Brunswick date with the Thornhill band: 'Don't Save Your Love for a Rainy Day'
382.s: Listening to the Brunswick session; she thinks it a date Claude needed a singer for and may revive the song.
382.ch: Early recordings and arrival in New York
382.q: That must've been one of those dates that Claude had and he needed a singer, so he just reached out and grabbed me.

70.t: John Nesbitt and the pickup McKinney's recording dates
70.s: Nesbitt arranged for McKinney's; when the band could not reach New York Redman recorded under its name with New York players like Hawkins, Fats Waller and Truehart.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: But there's so many trumpet players, you know, that you, that I have known. John Nesbitt was a great trumpet player to me.

18.s: Asked about Jersey Lightning and other titles, he repeats that his first record was the Oliver date with Russell's band.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson

418.t: His first record: the vocal with Luis Russell and microphone fright
418.s: John Nesbitt took him to the session; he was uncredited and nervous, has always feared microphones but likes a megaphone.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: Yeah. Well, you know, it was a (?) thing, when they... I guess when I contracted to play that number. But already, they didn't give me credit for singing. Which I wasn't a very good singer, I'll tell you that.

386.t: First record, 'Nasty But Nice', for Brunswick in 1929
386.s: On returning to Dallas he records for J. Mayo Williams, with Bert Johnson on trombone.
386.q: Cozy Cole. And Milt Hinton. And the next thing that I knew, somebody was calling me, wanting me to go to Europe. It's a funny thing, though, that I told you that I knew that guy's name that played the trombone with us on "Nasty But Nice," right? When I returned to Dallas I could not sit still, so…

235.t: First recordings: J.C. Heard, Etta Jones and Trummy Young
235.s: His first sessions were with J.C. Heard for RCA Victor, then a Trummy Young date arranged by Jimmy Jones around 1946-47, with Open the Door Richard a later date.
235.q: No, we were doing some dates when I was there. We did some things behind Etta Jones, for RCA Victor. Then I did some things with Trummy Young which John Levy did before he became George Shearing's manager and Jimmy Jones and Ray Nance. I don't know what ever happened to them. Bob Thiele produced…

74.t: Sunnyside Horseshoe and the first recordings in 1940
74.s: After the fire he moves to the Horseshoe and begins recording in 1940.
74.ch: Queens Terrace, Decca records and Amen
74.q: That's right, the latter part of '39, and we went across the street, where we got burned out, and that's when we went into Sunnyside Horseshoe and that's where I had Don Stovall.

30.t: The discography compiled by a French doctor
30.s: Dr. Kochlin of Paris gave him a discography running from 1926 to the sixties, with first recording in 1926 with Luis Russell and sessions with Jelly Roll Morton and Johnny Dodds, and tunes he had forgotten.
30.q: because I didn't even know him. In fact, he brought that and I thought he had forgotten it on the desk, but he said, "No, I brought that for you." I said, "Oh, thank you."

6.t: First record dates and why they were just another job
6.s: His first record was with pianist J. C. Johnson, followed by Clarence Williams dates; he explains he was never excited by records or fame and always thought he could do better.
6.ch: Early records, Detroit and Prohibition-era nightlife
6.q: Yeah, I understand he is. Well, he was the first one I made a record with. Yeah. Yeah. Then I -- well, all during this time I was making records here and there. Clarence Williams I made a few with, and other people, you know, who were, you know, small, you know.

81.t: The first song and the Ethel Waters Black Swan session
81.s: At the end of a day of Black Swan recording the musicians left, so Johnson played for Ethel Waters with cloth to muffle the piano, his first record.
81.ch: Porch interview and Jazz Train plans
81.q: Ninety percent of them. They were all songwriters. See, I was in a group of songwriter during that time and I pulled together -- I organized (inaudible).

98.t: Records with Lil Armstrong and Okeh, and his own name with Joe Williams
98.s: He recorded with Lil Armstrong's Decca band in the 1930s and in the late 1940s began recording for Okeh under his own name, including with Joe Williams.
98.ch: Big band, Chicago players, recordings and gospel
98.q: Right, right, right. And -- but after that, really, I didn't -- and in the '40s I went into a recording, and I started with Okeh record company, and I made records with them.

79.t: Babe's first records with Clarence Williams
79.s: Babe recalls her first recordings in 1938 for Clarence Williams, made with Connie Berry and Cozy, and Joe talks about taping tunes at home.
79.ch: Louis Armstrong, King Oliver and St. Louis memories
79.q: Have the flowers when you could smell them. Well, we had a situation happen ... I didn't know too much about it and Babe and I had gotten a little tape recorder and put out our records. She loved Louis. She loved Louis musically and so we wanted to tape our tunes so we recorded together just
